page: Microsoft Azure FX16-8ms_v2 is a specialized virtual machine driven by an Intel Xeon 8573C processor operating at 4.2 GHz on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is built on the x86_64 architecture, providing 8 dedicated vCPUs across 4 physical cores with 2 threads per core. Hardware acceleration flags include AVX, AVX-512, and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX). Cache architecture features 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and an extensive 260 MB L3 cache. System memory is sized at 336.0 GB, resulting in an exceptionally high allocation of 42.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage and contains no discrete GPUs.

Benchmark measurements indicate strong single-threaded processing capabilities driven by the 4.2 GHz clock frequency. The system achieved a Geekbench single-core score of 2338.0 and a text processing score of 2975.0, both placing in the top ten percent of tested servers. Compression throughput is notably strong, reaching 34.77 GB/sec for single-threaded gzip compression and 14.31 GB/sec for single-threaded bzip3 decompression. Due to the 8-vCPU topology, multi-threaded results remain in the middle tier, including a Geekbench multi-core score of 8962.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 15732.28. Memory bandwidth achieves 64.79 GB/sec for large uncached read operations and 44.95 GB/sec for large write operations.

From a resource and efficiency standpoint, the hardware profile pairs high single-core compute performance with an unusually large memory footprint on a low core count. This design offers qualitative cost efficiency for environments constrained by per-core software licensing frameworks, as memory-heavy operations can scale without licensing large quantities of compute cores. The operational tradeoffs include total dependence on remote storage solutions and lower throughput for heavily threaded parallel tasks, as illustrated by lower token generation rates on larger language models.

The FX16-8ms_v2 is targeted at memory-intensive workloads that demand high per-core execution speeds rather than massive thread concurrency. Suitable operational scenarios include large in-memory databases, electronic design automation (EDA), in-memory caching tiers, financial modeling, and licensed enterprise enterprise software.
